Q: Which is the best approach for faster API request and response handling in react js UI? A:

Generally vanilla JS is the fastest option. So you should start over without any frontend library. For the API you'd also want to use a language that was designed with performance in mind. I'm afraid you'll have to rewrite it in a new language. Consider C, Zig, or Rust, for example.

Take a look at Supercat (spc). It does both ANSI and HTML highlighting and can be configured for your particular output. It comes with some configuration files for source code files in C and Python, for example and log files, Changelogs, diffs and others.

Q: How to convert output of pwelch() into amplitude response in MATLAB A:

I have a simple sinusoid with amplitude of 1, but pwelch() gives me a different peak value.

1.- You are comparing amplitude with power directly.

Signal Power is the square of the amplitude over an impedance.

For simple academic exercises such impedance is assumed 1. But you still have to square the amplitude to compare time signals against command pwelch results.

How does command pwelch work : https://www.mathworks.com/help/signal/ref/pwelch.html

As far as I know, Welch's method is just an averaged squared DFT with a window function (Hamming in MATLAB). So, I took a square root to the output after dividing it by window length (for some reason it was dependent on window length), but the resultant amplitude is 0.605, not 1 (the amplitude of sine wave).

2.- pwelch returns the Power Spectrum Density estimate of x at frequencies f (rad/sample) :

All different ways to call pwelch :

    pxx = pwelch(x)
    [pxx,f] = pwelch(x,win,nOverlap,freqSpec)
    [pxx,f] = pwelch(x,win,nOverlap,freqSpec,Fs)
    [___] = pwelch(___,freqRange,spectrumType,trace)
    [___,pxxc] = pwelch(___,ConfidenceLevel=p)
    [___] = pwelch(___,Parent=h)

A Periodogram is just the Fourier transform of a time signal.

Call it Direct Fourier Transform (DFT), or Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), it doesn't matter. FFT is just a fast and efficient way to perform a DFT.

Note that there are better ways to estimate signal spetrum like the Wavelet transform.

The PSD of a stationary time signal x is the FFT of the autocorrelation of x : you correlate x on itself and run a DFT, or FFT.

Note that I have mentioned "stationary".

The spectrum has to be "stable" enough, not changing to fast so that the PSD is meaningful.

This is why time signals are windowed, so that short enough segments of the time signal are "slow enough" so that the obtained spectrum is meaningful.

Time Window too short? wasting resources because many adjacent spectrum samples are basically the same.

Time Window too long? Losing information. The spectrum is going to be static when it should be shifting to keep pace with time changes.

Since time signal is time variant, so it is the spectrum. But the time windowing of x determines the quality of the obtained spectrum.

pwelch is the first PSD estimation method taught in Signal Processing literature.

There are other power spectrum estimation methods through sliding time windows that all have to be "not too narrow" and at the same time "not too long" to keep pace with time signal changes, and translate such changes in real time to the equivalent spectrum of the signal.

3.- I have tried for different window lengths and the result is not dependent on the window length, as long as the overlap is smaller than the window, and the window is smaller than the total amount of samples available.

4.- Note that the "frequencies" returned by pwelch have units [rad/sample], not [Hz]. Command pwelch returns normalised angular frequencies, this is, within frequency span [0 pi] only, not [Hz].

To translate [rad/sample] normalised frequencies to Herz divide by 2*pi :

    f [cycle/sample] = 1/(2*pi) * w[rad/sample]

It was not dependent on any other parameters, like sampling rate, frequency, etc., and I eventually had to multiply it with 1.65 to make it 1.

5.- The single-side power spectrum of an amplitude 1, single tone is not 1, but 0.5 .

The two-side (power) spectrum of the same signal has 2 tones each of amplitude 0.25 .

pwelch allows to obtain both single-sided and double-sided spectrums.

Real time signals (no complex values) have symmetric spectrums, which is why the spectrum can be folded around the f=0 origin, doubling the obtained values, thus you have to divide by 2 on folding, or multiply by 2 if cutting negative frequencies off, to keep same signal power.

Signal power of time signals and their respective spectrums must be the same.

So, why is it not giving me the original amplitude? I also looked up for power compensation factor from using different window functions, but nothing matched to 1.65. Can anybody explain this to me?

6.- There's no need to divide by 2 the fs as you do in your call to pwelch.

Don't try to find "power compensation factors" either.

It doesn't work like this, trying to find a coefficient to link amplitudes to spectrum power values, that it can be done, but it is already done by command pwelch.

Following some scripts that I hope help understand where the problem is coming from :

6.1.- Random Mean Square

    dt=.0001;t1=0;t2=1;
    f_s=1/dt;

    t = [t1:dt:t2-dt];
    f0=100;
    x = cos(2*pi*f0*t);
    T=1/f0
    N=floor(f_s/f0)
    x_rms = rms(x)
    E=dt*sum(x([1:N]).^2)              % [W*s]=[J] general signal energy
    P=1/(2*N+1)*sum(x([1:N]).^2)       % [W] general signal power

.

x is, must be, a cyclic signal for this way of measuring power spectrum to work.

To avoid mixing the time window into power calculations one has to focus on 1 cycle only or a whole (natural, positive integer) multiple of 1 cycle.

Applying the general non-periodic, non-cyclic, definitions of signal energy and signal power to cyclic signals yields nonsense results

    E_N=sum(x.^2)
    P_N=1/(2*N+1)*E_N

The windowing effect : When not taking the right window, a multiple of the samples per cycle, Energy and Power turn dependent on the amount of samples, that should not be.

6.2.- Signal Power of broadband signals

But real signals are seldom pure tones.

In fact all modern wireless modulations tend to "spread" the payload over all the available channel bandwidth so when narrow interference happens, the damage to the payload can be fixed.

This is the standard Mathworks example to show how to measure signal power by measuring the the power spectrum that a signal generates over a known bandwidth :

    N = 1200;
    Fs = 1000;                 % sampling frequency
    t = (0:N-1)/Fs;
    sigma = 0.01;
    rng('default')

    s = chirp(t,100,1,300)+sigma*randn(size(t));

    pRMS = rms(s)^2

    powbp = bandpower(s,Fs,[0 Fs/2])
    obw(s,Fs);

    [wd,lo,hi,power] = obw(s,Fs);
    powtot = power/0.99;

    Fs = 3600;
    t = 0:1/Fs:2-1/Fs;
    x = sin(2*pi*60*t);
    y = polyval(ones(1,4),x) + randn(size(x));

    thd(y,Fs);

    pwrTot = bandpower(y,Fs,[0 Fs/2]);
    Harmonic = {'Fundamental';'First';'Second'};
    Freqs = [60 120 180]';
    Power = zeros([3 1]);
    for k = 1:3
       Power(k) = bandpower(y,Fs,Freqs(k)+[-10 10]);
    end
    s
    Percent = Power/pwrTot*100;
    in_dBW = pow2db(Power);
    in_dBmW=in_dBW+30;
    T = table(Freqs,Power,Percent,in_dBW,in_dBmW,'RowNames',Harmonic)

6.3.- How to call pwelch

I have modified the way you call pwelch so the correct power spectrum is obtained :

    fs = 2000;
    win_len = 500;
    t = 1/fs:1/fs:win_len;
    welch_win_len = 400;
    N = length(t);

    % target signal
    amplitude = 1;
    target_f = 10;
    x = amplitude*sin(2*pi*target_f*t);

    Prms=rms(x)^2

    Pbp = bandpower(x,fs,[0 fs/2])

    [Pxx, f_welch] =   pwelch(x,win_len,welch_win_len,fs,"onesided","power","mean",ConfidenceLevel=.95);

    figure(1);
    plot(f_welch, Pxx);

    grid on;

.

The results of this closing script are as expected

    Prms =
   0.500000000000000
    Pbp =
   0.500000000000107

.

Prms is the signal power directly calculated using time samples.

Pbd is the power calculated from the spectrum.

Further reading :

https://uk.mathworks.com/help/signal/ug/practical-introduction-to-frequency-domain-analysis.html

Q: How can I apply a specific stash entry? A:

If you have more stashes I recommend you to check before you will apply them. Use:

git stash show -p

to see the last stash in detail. If you have more stashes and you want a specific one then add a number of stash at the end:

git stash show 1

Then when you find the right stash apply it by typing:

git stash apply 1

Again the number is an example without number you will apply the last one.

Q: Get maintenance mode status A:

In 2026 there's an artisan command to retrieve maintenance mode :

php artisan about | grep "Maintenance"

It gives you the following output :

  Maintenance Mode ............................................................................................................................. OFF

Q: Can't get on-board LED to blink A:

It seems that your original code is already correct. Not every ESP32 development board has an onboard LED connected to GPIO 2. First, you should check whether the LED on your development board is actually connected to GPIO 2 or to another GPIO pin.

If the LED is connected to a different pin, you can simply update the GPIO number in your original code and run it again.

In your updated code, you included the built-in printf() function. This function works with the ESP32 serial interface, and some development boards include serial debugging LEDs. Because of this, you might think the code is working correctly since the LED blinks when printf() is used, but that is not necessarily the case.

My advice is to first check your development board and identify the correct GPIO pin connected to the onboard LED.
